item.title: Pope will meet with survivors of clergy abuse during upcoming trip to Latin America, Vatican says
item.description:
Pope will meet with survivors of clergy abuse during upcoming trip to Latin America, Vatican says
The Vatican says Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin AmericaByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 12:05 PM
Share
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin America, which will take the American pope to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, the Vatican said Tuesday.
The Vatican statement didn’t say when the encounters would take place or where, but said “several meetings are planned,” suggesting more than one encounter. The Nov. 6-17 trip is going ahead as planned despite Leo's Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery which had put the trip in question.
Continuing the practice of his two recent predecessors, Leo met with abuse survivors in June in Spain and most recently in France. Ahead of the French trip, the Vatican confirmed the meeting ahead of time rather than after it took place, as had been the previous practice.
“These meetings reflect the pope’s desire to express his solidarity with those who have suffered and continue to suffer as a result of this violence, to work with them to build paths to healing that are accessible to anyone in need, and to ensure that the church is a safe and spiritually healthy place that lives out and communicates the Gospel,” according to a Vatican statement Tuesday.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru, and he saw first-hand the effects of abuse on victims. He was the designated bishop in the Peruvian bishops conference to hear from victims of an influential but abusive movement, the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.

item.title: Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
item.description:
Swiss Ebola patient in Nigeria evacuated to Switzerland
A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria has been medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husbandByDYEPKAZAH SHIBAYAN Associated Press and MARK BANCHEREAU Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 9:13 AM
Share
ABUJA, Nigeria -- A Swiss woman being treated for Ebola in Nigeria was medically evacuated to Switzerland with her husband Monday, officials said, as Nigerian authorities continued monitoring 52 people who had been in contact with her.
Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Pate said the woman, the country’s first case in the current outbreak, left the capital, Abuja, early Monday with his approval. Her condition had improved significantly, and she was stable, conscious and able to communicate, he said.
“This does not mean she is not still infectious, hence the strict protocols in place,” Pate wrote on X. Her husband, a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria, has shown no symptoms.
The World Health Organization’s regional director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, said the evacuation was arranged because the couple are Swiss citizens and that Nigerian medical teams had stabilized the woman after treating her through the acute phase of the illness.
Switzerland will take over her care and monitor her husband, while Nigeria will continue following 52 other contacts, Janabi said.
“With the evacuation of the patient and her husband, Nigeria currently has no Ebola cases,” he said, stressing that vigilance remained critical.
Pate said containment measures remained in place and urged Nigerians to remain vigilant.
The woman tested positive after returning to Abuja from Uganda. Nigerian authorities said Friday they had yet to establish how she contracted the virus.
Switzerland’s foreign ministry told The Associated Press that she had not visited Congo and was believed to have been infected while traveling to Uganda with her husband.

item.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo's Latin America trip after post-surgery checkup
item.description:
Vatican confirms Pope Leo's Latin America trip after post-surgery checkup
Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru.ByThe Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 12:53 PM
VATICAN CITY -- VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will proceed with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, after doctors determined there are no medical reasons preventing him from traveling three weeks after lung cancer surgery, the Vatican confirmed Monday.
The Vatican press office said the pope’s recovery continues to progress in line with favorable assessments from his medical team. It also confirmed the pope is keeping the already ambitious trip program with no announced changes.
Surgeons on Oct. 13 removed a lobe where the nodule later diagnosed as malignant was located, in the first major health event of Leo's 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer.
Since returning to the Vatican, Leo has gradually resumed his activities while adjusting his schedule to prioritize recovery and periods of rest, the statement said.
The pope’s physician, Luigi Carbone, said there's no medical reason preventing Leo's trip to South America, which involves a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.

item.title: A cartoonist takes Japan’s new imperial succession law to court over male-only heirs
item.description:
A cartoonist takes Japan’s new imperial succession law to court over male-only heirs
A popular Japanese cartoonist has sued the government over a revised imperial succession lawByMARI YAMAGUCHI Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 10:39 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
TOKYO -- A popular Japanese cartoonist who has written books on history and monarchy has sued the government over a revised imperial succession law allowing royals to adopt male relatives from former branch families to father future heirs.
The revised law took effect Saturday despite criticism over the male-only succession rules in Japan's 1,500-year-old monarchy. Next in line after Emperor Naruhito is his younger brother Akishino, followed by the emperor's 20-year-old nephew, Prince Hisahito. There are no other eligible heirs in his generation.
The revised law allows adoption of unmarried male descendants, aged 15 or older, of distant imperial relatives, but only through an unbroken male line, into a branch of the royal family. They would not be able to inherit the throne themselves, but their heirs would be eligible.
Four of the 11 former branch families who renounced their royal status in 1947 remain. Officials say they are at least 36 generations removed from Naruhito after splitting from a common male-line ancestor 600 years ago. Critics say they are too distant to be considered relatives.
In his lawsuit, Yoshinori Kobayashi says the adoption of former royals, who are commoners, discriminates against other commoners in violation of Article 14 of the constitution, which guarantees equality regardless of “race, creed, sex, social status or family origin.”
"The adoption would introduce a new class system of ‘former imperial branch family’ in Japan. ... It's a serious problem," Kobayashi told reporters after filing the lawsuit with the Tokyo District Court, a first legal step against the revised law. No trial date has been set.

item.title: Singer Chris Brown to be sentenced over bottle attack at a London nightclub
item.description:
Singer Chris Brown to be sentenced over bottle attack at a London nightclub
Chris Brown has avoided prison time for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years agoByBRIAN MELLEY Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 2:13 AM
Share
LONDON -- Grammy-winning singer Chris Brown avoided prison time Monday for beating a music producer with a tequila bottle at a London nightclub three years ago.
The 37-year-old was given an eight-month sentence, suspended for a year.
He had faced up to three years in prison after pleading guilty to a count of affray in July for the attack on the dance floor of Tape, a private club in the swanky Mayfair neighborhood in February 2023.
Video footage played in court showed Brown having to be pulled away from the victim, his former friend Abraham Diaw, after striking him twice in the head with a bottle.
“The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained,” Judge Tony Baumgartner said in Southwark Crown Court.
Despite the seriousness of the attack, Baumgartner said Brown did not qualify for a custodial sentence because he pleaded guilty and there were several mitigating circumstances, including stable employment and charity work. The judge acknowledged Brown’s previous convictions but said he had maintained a clean record in recent years.
Brown has faced repeated legal trouble since his felony conviction in the 2009 assault of his then-girlfriend, Rihanna, hours before the pair were due to perform at the Grammys.
He has been arrested in several U.S. states over altercations but was either not charged or prosecutors later dropped the charges. In 2019 he was arrested in Paris and questioned on suspicion of rape, but was released without charge.

item.title: Caribbean seeks reparations and questions role of monarchy before King Charles visits
item.description:
Caribbean seeks reparations and questions role of monarchy before King Charles visits
The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heardByDÁNICA COTO Associated Press and JOHN MYERS JR. Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 12:11 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico -- The royals are coming, and the Caribbean wants to be heard.
Islanders are seeking slavery reparations from Britain, a formal apology for its role in the slave trade and greater independence from the former colonial power.
The Bahamas National Reparations Committee said it already knows what awaits the Caribbean as King Charles III and Queen Camilla prepare for this week's trip: “Schools emptied of children who will stand in the sun and wave for the Crown that has taken everything from their ancestors and comes back smiling.”
Charles is expected to visit the Bahamas on Tuesday to begin the nine-day trip to the Caribbean. His last official visit to the archipelago was in July 1973 as a prince who granted the Bahamas independence, ending 300 years of British rule. But the Bahamas remains a Commonwealth realm, along with six other Caribbean nations that recognize Charles as their king and head of state.
While in the Bahamas, Charles is scheduled to visit Clifford Park, where the archipelago’s black, turquoise and yellow flag was raised for the first time more than half a century ago.
His visit will raise important questions, said Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, chair of the Bahamas National Reparations Committee.
“Why do we still have a king? What does this person really represent to us? Why is he coming and how will that benefit us?” she said.
A psychology professor at the University of the Bahamas, Campbell-Dean said she recently mentioned Charles’ upcoming visit to her students, and they were not excited. She responded: “I know y’all might not care about this man who is coming, but here’s why this is of importance.”

item.title: Serbia’s victorious student movement faces tough challenges as it prepares to take power
item.description:
Serbia’s victorious student movement faces tough challenges as it prepares to take power
Serbia’s youth movement pulled out a stunning election victory at the weekend against the country’s long-time strongman ruler Aleksandar VucicByJOVANA GEC Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 11:27 AM
Share
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbia's youth movement pulled out a stunning election victory against the country's long-time strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic. But turning its promises of sweeping democratic reforms into reality could prove far more difficult.
The leaderless and diverse movement with few candidates with experience in politics has promised to root out corruption, free the media and guarantee the rule of law it says have been ravaged during Vucic's 14 years in power.
Though armed with a strong mandate for change stemming from a convincing election victory, a new government will still encounter a myriad of hurdles along the way. Expectations are running high and so is impatience after public discontent built over years.
Here is a look at the challenges that lie ahead:
Though Vucic conceded defeat just an hour and a half after polls closed on Sunday, it's likely to take weeks before a new government is formed.
Serbia's election laws provide for a period of appeals and potential reruns at individual polling stations before final election results are announced and a new Parliament is inaugurated. Any meaningful policy changes can only take place after a new government takes office.
Serbia’s state election commission so far has released only preliminary and incomplete results of the vote on Sunday, but they are unlikely to change much — the Students’ List is set to have a comfortable majority of 140 seats in the 250-member Parliament while Vucic’s SNS party will have 104.

item.title: A tornado rips through a construction site in Turkey, killing 4 workers
item.description:
A tornado rips through a construction site in Turkey, killing 4 workers
A tornado has hit a construction site in Antalya, Turkey, killing four workers and injuring anotherByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 7:13 AM
Share
ANTALYA, Turkey -- A tornado hit a construction site in the Mediterranean coastal province of Antalya early on Tuesday, destroying a container housing workers and killing four of them, an official said.
A fifth worker, who was staying inside another container, was injured in the powerful storm that struck the building site in Antalya’s Kepez district, Gov. Hulusi Sahin told reporters.
Three of the workers who were killed were Syrian nationals, Sahin said. There was no immediate information on the condition of the injured worker.
The tornado, which came shortly after the country’s weather agency warned of heavy rains, also knocked down a crane at the site, Sahin said.

item.title: In Serbia and Hungary, groundswells of youthful energy topple entrenched governments
item.description:
In Serbia and Hungary, groundswells of youthful energy topple entrenched governments
Serbia has seen a dramatic shift after President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to student-backed candidatesByJOVANA GEC Associated Press and JUSTIN SPIKE Associated PressOctober 26, 2026, 11:32 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
BELGRADE, Serbia -- For over a year, residents of Serbia's capital were blocked from entering one of the city's most prominent parks, nestled between Parliament and the offices of the powerful right-wing leader, Aleksandar Vucic.
The reason: the park in Belgrade had been cordoned off and occupied by throngs of Vucic's most ardent — and violent — supporters, an effective enforcer squad for the authoritarian leader tasked with intimidating and sometimes assaulting members of a growing anti-government student movement.
But after Vucic stunned the Balkan country Sunday evening by conceding defeat in an election against student-backed candidates, ecstatic young revelers filled the streets of Belgrade and ripped down the cordons around the encampment known as Caciland. Before long, the barricades lay tossed aside and the tents within went up in smoke, along with Vucic's power.
The seismic shift came after two years of relentless organizing and sustained protests by the student movement, which accused the Kremlin-backed Vucic of increasing authoritarianism, connections to organized crime and runaway corruption.
It also echoed other bottom-up, youth-led protest movements that have recently challenged what they see as entrenched, unresponsive power structures in Europe and beyond. Close to home, in neighboring Hungary, they succeeded in ousting another entrenched leader.

item.title: Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader ends hunger strike after meeting with his brother
item.description:
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader ends hunger strike after meeting with his brother
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu has ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brotherByKHALED KAZZIHA Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 10:59 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ended a brief hunger strike Tuesday after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brother, his lead lawyer said.
Lissu, who survived being shot 16 times in a 2017 assassination attempt and has spent periods in exile citing threats to his life, leads Tanzania’s main opposition party, Chadema.
He faces a treason charge carrying a possible death sentence and has been detained for more than 18 months, with a final judgment scheduled for Nov. 6.
His lead lawyer, Rugemeleza Nshala, told The Associated Press by telephone that Lissu had planned to begin the strike Monday to protest restrictions on court-ordered confidential legal consultations. He postponed it after prison authorities promised private access.
When those consultations failed to take place Monday, Lissu began refusing food Tuesday morning, Nshala said.
“Lissu did not take his tea, breakfast or lunch,” Nshala said. He ended the strike after lunchtime following the private meeting with his brother.
Prison authorities and the government had issued no public statements on the hunger strike.
Nshala said Saturday that prison authorities had, on some occasions, barred access to Lissu altogether. He expressed concern about the health implications of a hunger strike because Lissu relies on medication.
Lissu was arrested April 9, 2025, after addressing a rally calling for electoral reforms ahead of that year’s general election and was charged with treason the following day.
